column5: Moses before Pharaoh; refusal to heed
column6: In the Bible’s Moses–Pharaoh scene, Pharaoh asks who YHWH is and says he will not obey YHWH’s voice or release Israel; this gives the commentary’s rejected summons to Pharaoh a concrete counterpart, while making Pharaoh’s claimed ignorance explicit.

column5: Pharaoh’s servants fear YHWH’s word
column6: The commentary says the one who fears takes the reminder; during the hail warning, Pharaoh’s servants who feared YHWH’s word hurried their servants and livestock to shelter, showing fear as heedful response.

column5: Failure to set the heart on the warning
column6: The next verse says those who did not set their heart on YHWH’s word left their servants and livestock in the field; it gives a precise refusal alongside the fear-led response in the preceding verse.

column5: Moses confronts Pharaoh’s refusal
column6: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh how long he will refuse to humble himself before YHWH and demand Israel’s release; this is the same ruler’s rejection of a divine summons, in the biblical narrative’s own terms.

column5: Hearing in order to learn fear
column6: Moses recalls the assembly at Horeb so Israel would hear God’s words and learn to fear him throughout life, then teach their children; hearing instruction is explicitly the path to the reverent fear the commentary associates with receiving the reminder.

column5: Warning and reward in keeping instruction
column6: The psalm says God’s rules warn the servant and that keeping them brings great reward; this joins an admonition’s warning function to a concrete benefit, as the commentary asks whether the reminder benefits.

column5: Wisdom calls and is refused
column6: Personified Wisdom says she called and was refused and stretched out her hand without being heeded; this gives the bedbaht’s avoidance of offered admonition a specific scriptural scene.

column5: Different responses to rebuke
column6: Proverbs says rebuking a scoffer brings hatred but rebuking a wise person brings love; like the commentary’s contrast between the one who takes the reminder and the one who avoids it, the response depends on the hearer.

column5: Instruction increases the wise hearer’s learning
column6: The verse says instruction makes the wise wiser and teaching increases the righteous person’s learning; it supplies a concrete account of how admonition benefits the receptive hearer.

column5: Listening to life-giving reproof
column6: The one whose ear listens to life-giving reproof dwells among the wise; this closely matches the commentary’s hearer who receives admonition through an inwardly responsive disposition.

column5: Ignoring instruction versus heeding reproof
column6: Proverbs contrasts the person who ignores instruction and harms himself with the one who heeds reproof and gains understanding, spelling out both sides of the commentary’s reception/avoidance contrast.

column5: Fear, wisdom, and turning from evil
column6: Job’s poem identifies fear of the Lord with wisdom and turning from evil with understanding; this brings together the commentary’s knowledge-inflected fear and the distance from wrongdoing suggested by its avoidance language.

column5: Trembling at God’s word
column6: Isaiah says the Lord looks toward the lowly and contrite person who trembles at his word; this gives a scriptural profile for the commentary’s inwardly trembling hearer who receives admonition.

column5: A warning intended to turn its hearers
column6: Jeremiah’s scroll is to recount coming disaster so Judah may hear, turn from evil, and be forgiven; the passage makes the intended benefit of a reminder explicit.

column5: Officials fear after hearing the scroll
column6: After Baruch reads Jeremiah’s words, the officials look at one another in fear and say they must report them to the king; the warning produces the kind of fear-led attention that the commentary associates with receiving counsel.

column5: The king burns the warning
column6: As the scroll is read, Jehoiakim cuts off its columns and burns them; the act gives a stark, material form to the commentary’s image of the wretched keeping the reminder at a distance.

column5: The king and his servants feel no fear
column6: The verse says the king and his servants were not afraid and did not tear their garments after hearing the words; it contrasts their response with the officials’ fear in 36:16 and shows refusal despite access to the warning.

column5: Whether the rebellious hear or refuse
column6: God tells Ezekiel that whether the rebellious house hears or refuses, its members will know a prophet has been among them; the message’s delivery is distinguished from its acceptance, as in the commentary’s divided audience.

column5: Speak the words whether heard or refused
column6: Ezekiel is told to speak God’s words whether the rebellious hear or refuse; this clarifies the admonisher’s task even where the reminder may not benefit its audience.

column5: The warned wicked person who will not turn
column6: The watchman is to warn the wicked; if the warned person does not turn, he dies in his iniquity while the watchman has delivered himself. This links offered warning, refusal, and consequence without making the messenger responsible for the hearer’s response.

column5: Hearing without doing
column6: The people come to Ezekiel, sit before him, and hear his words, yet do not do them; their mouths show love while their hearts pursue gain. This complicates a simple hear/refuse split by showing outward attendance without inward reception.

column5: Turning away and stopping the ears
column6: Zechariah says the ancestors refused to pay attention, turned a stubborn shoulder, and stopped their ears; the bodily gestures make the commentary’s language of passing by an admonition concrete.

column5: A hardened heart that will not hear
column6: The people made their hearts hard lest they hear the Torah and the words sent through earlier prophets, bringing great wrath; the verse ties refusal of warning to a chosen incapacity to receive it.

column5: Nineveh receives Jonah’s warning
column6: After Jonah announces Nineveh’s overthrow, its people believe God, fast, and put on sackcloth; their response gives a narrative instance of warning being received and changing its hearers.

column5: God relents after seeing Nineveh’s response
column6: The narrative says God saw that the Ninevites turned from their evil way and did not bring the announced disaster; this completes the warning’s benefit in the story with a changed outcome.

column5: Josiah hears the book and tears his clothes
column6: When the king hears the words of the book of the law, he tears his clothes; the scene offers a concrete example of a hearer registering a warning rather than passing it by.

column5: A humbled response to heard words
column6: Huldah says Josiah’s heart was tender and he humbled himself when he heard the words against Jerusalem, so God heard him; this makes inward responsiveness and its consequence explicit.

column5: Despising words until judgment
column6: The chronicler says the people mocked God’s messengers, despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets until wrath came; it is a concentrated account of rejecting repeated admonition and its outcome.

column5: Those who fear speak to one another
column6: Malachi describes those who fear YHWH speaking with one another while YHWH listens and records them; this turns the commentary’s fear-led reception into a communal exchange whose hearers are remembered by God.

column5: Hearing and doing the sayings of Jesus
column6: Jesus compares the one who hears his words and does them to a house built on rock; it gives a concrete outcome for receiving instruction rather than merely encountering it.

column5: Hearing without doing
column6: Jesus contrasts the person who hears his words but does not do them with the wise builder; the foolish house’s collapse makes the consequence of non-reception concrete.

column5: Closed ears and an unhealed hearer
column6: Matthew’s quotation of Isaiah describes a people whose heart has grown dull and ears are hard, so they do not hear, understand, turn, and receive healing; it gives a scriptural account of refusal as blocked reception.

column5: Hearing, accepting, and bearing fruit
column6: In the sower parable, good soil represents those who hear the word, accept it, and bear fruit; this supplies a specific picture of a reminder that benefits its hearer.

column5: Refusal of Moses and the Prophets
column6: In the rich man’s story, Abraham says that those who do not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead; the warning cannot be made effective by a more spectacular sign when prior admonition is refused.

column5: One proclamation, opposed receptions
column6: Paul says the word of the cross is foolishness to those perishing but God’s power to those being saved; one proclamation divides hearers by reception and outcome, like the commentary’s two responses.

column5: The message among those saved and perishing
column6: Paul calls the apostolic mission Christ’s fragrance among both those being saved and those perishing; the shared proclamation reaches audiences whose outcomes differ, adding a Christian account of divided reception.

column5: A fragrance from death or from life
column6: Paul specifies that the same fragrance is for one person from death to death and for another from life to life; this sharpens the commentary’s contrast between the person who receives the reminder and the one who avoids it.

column5: Daily exhortation against a hardened heart
column6: Hebrews tells the community to exhort one another every day so no one is hardened by sin’s deceit; admonition is a mutual practice meant to keep hearers receptive.

column5: Hearing without hardening
column6: Hebrews repeats, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts”; this directly joins hearing a divine summons to the choice between receiving it and resisting it.

column5: The message that did not benefit its hearers
column6: Hebrews says the good news heard by the wilderness generation did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith; this closely parallels the commentary’s question of whether the reminder benefits and makes faith the interpretive bridge.

column5: Doers rather than hearers only
column6: James warns readers not to be hearers only who deceive themselves, but to do the word; this distinguishes exposure to instruction from receiving it in practice.

column5: The preacher’s duty to reprove and exhort
column6: Timothy is charged to proclaim the word and to reprove, rebuke, and exhort with patience; this gives a concrete Christian formulation of the admonisher’s task even when response varies.

column5: A hearer who will not endure sound teaching
column6: Paul says people will not endure sound teaching and will gather teachers to suit their desires; this describes avoidance as actively selecting away from admonition.

column5: Turning the ears from truth
column6: Paul says they will turn their ears away from truth and toward myths; the bodily image of turning away closely specifies the commentary’s image of keeping the reminder at a distance.

column5: Mockery and postponement after Paul’s announcement
column6: In Athens, some mock when Paul speaks of resurrection, while others say they will hear him again; the scene records distinct responses to a public religious summons.

column5: Some hearers join and believe
column6: The following verse names people who join Paul and believe; it completes the same scene with the response of hearers who accept the proclamation.

column5: Arabic ذ ك ر and Hebrew זכר
column6: The commentary labels the Arabic source root ذ ك ر and frames dhikrā as admonition; Hebrew זכר (zakar, “remember”) is cognate, and Moses uses it to command Israel to remember the wilderness road as a lesson in humility and keeping the commandments. The connection is the remembered lesson, not an equation of memory with admonition.

column5: Choosing life rather than death
column6: Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life; this gives a specific choice-and-consequence frame alongside the commentary’s contrast between the wretched and the opposite of happiness.

column5: A blessed person refuses wicked counsel
column6: The psalm calls blessed the person who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked; unlike the bedbaht who avoids divine admonition, this person’s distance is good because of what is refused, making the object of avoidance decisive.

column5: Fear as the beginning of wisdom
column6: The psalm says fear of YHWH is the beginning of wisdom and that those who practice the commands have good understanding; it links fear and knowledge in the reverse direction from the commentary’s claim that fear commonly arises from knowledge.

column5: Eliphaz calls the reproved person happy
column6: Eliphaz says the person whom God reproves is happy and should not despise divine discipline; this touches the commentary’s contrast between the bedbaht and happiness, while remaining Eliphaz’s counsel within Job’s debate rather than an unqualified narrator verdict.

column5: Rejected knowledge and unchosen fear
column6: Wisdom’s opponents are said to hate knowledge and not choose fear of YHWH; alongside the commentary’s Arabic source note linking خشية to “I knew” and its claim that fear commonly arises from knowledge, Proverbs gives the relation in the opposite pedagogical direction.

column5: The listener’s security
column6: Wisdom says whoever listens will dwell securely and be at ease without dread of disaster; this adds safety as the outcome of attending to counsel, while the commentary emphasizes the receiver’s fear as the disposition that makes listening possible.

column5: The word accomplishes its purpose
column6: Isaiah compares God’s word to rain and snow that do not return without watering the earth, saying the word accomplishes God’s purpose; beside the commentary’s “if the reminder benefits,” this presents divine speech as effective, though not necessarily beneficial to every hearer.

column5: Those who tremble at the word amid hostility
column6: Isaiah addresses hearers who tremble at YHWH’s word and then describes brothers who hate and expel them; this places reverent reception amid social hostility, a sharper conflict than the commentary’s brief contrast of receiver and avoider.

column5: An offered way rejected by its hearers
column6: Jeremiah urges people to seek the good ancient path and walk in it, but they answer that they will not; the scene makes rejection of offered guidance explicit.

column5: A prophet heard as a pleasant song
column6: Ezekiel says his hearers treat his words like a beautiful song and listen without doing them; the image adds a form of non-reception in which people enjoy the sound of admonition while its claim passes them by.

column5: Rejected knowledge and forgotten instruction
column6: Hosea says the people are destroyed for lack of knowledge because they rejected knowledge and forgot God’s teaching; it connects the commentary’s knowledge-and-fear discussion to the consequence of refusing instruction.

column5: Arabic dhikrā and Hebrew זכרון
column6: The commentary labels Arabic ذ ك ر as its source root and uses dhikrā for admonition; Malachi’s זכרון (zikaron, “remembrance”) uses the cognate Hebrew root for the record of those who fear YHWH and speak together, where the sense is memorial rather than instruction.

column5: Fearers reinterpreted as paired Torah learners
column6: The Mishnah reads Malachi’s people who fear God and speak together as two who sit with words of Torah between them, with the divine presence among them; this rabbinic interpretation turns fearful reception into shared study, echoing the commentary’s description of admonition as passing to another.

column5: Fear as wisdom’s beginning
column6: Ben Sira says fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; alongside the commentary’s account of fear as reverent and associated with knowledge, this Jewish wisdom text makes fear the entry into wisdom rather than its result.

column5: Listening yields knowledge
column6: Ben Sira says the one who loves listening gains knowledge and the attentive person becomes wise; this gives a concise account of instruction benefiting a receptive hearer.

column5: Disciples blessed with seeing and hearing
column6: Jesus tells his disciples their eyes and ears are blessed because they see and hear; this supplies the positive counterpart to the dull hearing in the preceding verse and to the commentary’s fear-led recipient.

column5: Joyful reception that does not last
column6: In the sower parable, rocky-ground hearers receive the word at once with joy but fall away when trouble comes; this preserves a secondary case beyond simple acceptance or avoidance, where initial reception fails to endure.

column5: Failure to see as imposed blindness
column6: Paul says the god of this age has blinded unbelievers’ minds so they cannot see the gospel’s light; this gives a different account of failed reception from the commentary’s active image of the wretched person avoiding the reminder.

column5: Doing the heard word brings blessing
column6: James describes the person who looks into the law and perseveres as a doer who will be blessed in doing; it specifies the benefit of receiving instruction as practice, not mere hearing.

column5: God’s outstretched hands to a disobedient people
column6: Paul quotes God’s all-day outstretched hands toward a disobedient and contrary people; the image pairs persistent invitation with refusal and gives a Christian rereading of Israel’s resistance to divine speech.

column5: Reproof as loving discipline
column6: The risen Christ says he reproves and disciplines those he loves, then urges repentance; this Christian text interprets correction as care and gives the admonition a restorative purpose.

column5: Noah’s preaching and the hearers saved
column6: Clement presents Noah as preaching repentance and says those who heeded were saved; this early Christian retelling makes the outcome of a received admonition explicit.

column5: The soils as different kinds of hearers
column6: Chrysostom’s homily on the sower reads the soils as differing hearers of the word; this Christian interpretation develops why one proclamation bears fruit in some and not in others, much like the commentary’s two responses to reminder.

column5: Nocturnal emission and exclusion from camp
column6: The commentary’s Arabic source note links junub with distance from prayer and the mosque; Deuteronomy orders a man with a nocturnal emission outside the camp until evening, a specific ritual-distance comparison, though its setting is the military camp and it says nothing about prayer.

column5: Washing and return at evening
column6: Deuteronomy continues that the man washes and returns to camp at sunset; this clarifies the temporary boundary behind the commentary’s junub association while differing from its prayer-and-mosque framing.
